cards.front: What is linkage, and why are two genes on the same chromosome usually inherited together?
cards.back: **Linkage** is the tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Whole chromosomes are sorted into gametes during meiosis, so the linked alleles travel as a unit.
cards.hint: Think about what meiosis moves into each gamete.

cards.front: How can crossing over stop linked alleles always travelling together?
cards.back: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes break and rejoin at matching positions, exchanging sections. A crossover between two loci makes **recombinant** chromatids carrying new allele combinations.
cards.hint: Which chromatids take part in the exchange?

cards.front: A test cross gives 800 offspring, and 120 of them are recombinant. What is the recombinant percentage?
cards.hint: Divide recombinant offspring by the total number of offspring.

cards.back: A **gene locus** is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome. Homologous chromosomes carry the same gene at the same locus.
A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, that carry the same genes at the same loci. Every gene is therefore present twice.
An **allele** is a version of a gene. One chromosome of a pair may carry allele A while its partner carries allele a.
cards.hint: Think about the two copies of a gene in a homologous pair.

cards.front: Why do genes on different chromosomes give a 9:3:3:1 ratio in a cross?
cards.back: Homologous pairs align and separate **independently** in meiosis I, so alleles combine freely. Unlinked genes therefore make four gamete types in equal numbers.
cards.hint: Compare where the two genes sit with the case of genes on one chromosome.

cards.front: What offspring ratio does a test cross of AaBb with aabb give for linked genes with no crossing over?
cards.back: **1:1**, with only the two parental phenotypes. The AaBb parent makes only AB and ab gametes, and the partner contributes only ab.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to assume linked alleles are always inherited together?
cards.back: Linkage is not complete, because crossing over can separate linked alleles. This is why a few recombinant offspring usually appear.

cards.front: Why does a smaller recombinant percentage mean two loci lie closer together?
cards.back: Crossovers fall at random along the chromosome, so one is less likely to fall between loci that are close together. Fewer gametes are recombinant as the loci get closer.
cards.hint: Think about where a crossover can land between two nearby loci.

cards.front: Why do very distant loci on one chromosome behave as if they were unlinked?
cards.back: Crossing over happens between them in most meioses, so recombinants approach 50%. This matches the pattern of independent assortment.
cards.hint: Consider how often a crossover falls between two far-apart loci.

cards.front: How do you identify the parental classes in a test cross result?
cards.back: The two largest classes are parental. They show which alleles shared a chromosome in the parent, and every other class is recombinant.
One of two identical copies of a replicated chromosome. The two chromatids are held together at the **centromere**.

cards.front: What does meiosis do to chromosome number?
cards.back: **Meiosis** halves the chromosome number and normally produces four genetically different cells. These cells form gametes.
